name: Zero Hour extra topics
about: 32 extra behaviour questions written by team 20, in the same shape as questions.json, on topics the supplied bank does not cover. The host can pick them in the team battle. All are general (phase_id is null).

questions.question: Your screen suddenly shows a message saying your files are locked and you must pay to get them back. What is this most likely to be?

options.A: A software update
options.B: Ransomware
options.C: A printer error
options.D: A password reminder

questions.explanation: Ransomware locks or encrypts files and demands payment. Recognising it quickly means it can be reported and contained before it spreads.

questions.question: An email from an unknown sender has an attachment called "Invoice.pdf.exe". What is the warning sign?

options.A: The file name has two extensions and ends in .exe, so it is a program
options.B: Invoices are always safe
options.C: It was sent during working hours
options.D: The email is short

questions.explanation: A double extension ending in .exe hides a program behind a harmless-looking name. Opening it can install malware.

questions.question: You think you may have opened a malicious file and your laptop is acting strangely. What should you do first?

options.A: Keep working and see if it gets better
options.B: Restart it several times
options.C: Disconnect from the network and report it to IT security straight away
options.D: Delete the file and tell nobody

questions.explanation: Disconnecting limits the spread and reporting quickly lets the security team respond. Hiding it gives malware more time to reach other systems.

questions.secure_behaviour: Never Pay or Bypass the Process
questions.question: A manager says the team should quietly pay a ransom from a project budget so the deadline is not missed. What is the secure response?

options.A: Pay quickly to save time
options.B: Pay half now and half later
options.C: Contact the attackers to negotiate
options.D: Escalate to the incident response team and follow the agreed plan

questions.explanation: Ransom decisions belong to the incident response plan, not an individual team. Paying does not guarantee recovery and may fund further attacks.

questions.question: Your laptop says security updates are ready to install. What is the best action?

options.A: Postpone them for months
options.B: Install them as soon as is practical
options.C: Turn off automatic updates
options.D: Only update when something breaks

questions.explanation: Security updates fix weaknesses attackers already know about. Delaying them leaves the door open.

questions.question: While browsing a news site, a pop-up says "Your browser is out of date, click here to download the update". What is the risk?

options.A: None, pop-ups are always genuine
options.B: It might slow the page down
options.C: It may be a fake update that installs malware
options.D: It will change your homepage

questions.explanation: Genuine updates come through the system or the official app, not website pop-ups. Fake updates are a common way to deliver malware.

questions.question: You need a tool for a task and find a free version on an unfamiliar website. What should you do?

options.A: Request it through IT or use the approved software catalogue
options.B: Download it as it is free
options.C: Ask a colleague to install it for you
options.D: Install it on your personal device and transfer files

questions.explanation: Approved software is checked and kept up to date. Unknown downloads can carry malware or never receive security fixes.

questions.secure_behaviour: Do Not Skip Updates Under Pressure
questions.question: A colleague asks you to keep delaying a critical update on a control-room PC because restarting is inconvenient. What should you do?

options.A: Delay it indefinitely
options.B: Uninstall the update service
options.C: Ignore the update messages
options.D: Agree a planned maintenance window with IT so it is installed safely

questions.explanation: Critical systems still need patching. Planning a window keeps operations running while closing known weaknesses.

questions.secure_behaviour: Do Not Plug In Unknown Devices
questions.question: You find a USB stick in the car park labelled "Salaries 2026". What should you do?

options.A: Plug it in to find the owner
options.B: Hand it to IT security or reception without plugging it in
options.C: Take it home
options.D: Plug it into a spare computer

questions.explanation: Dropped USB sticks are a known trick to get malware inside a building. Curiosity is exactly what the attacker is counting on.

questions.question: A visitor at a conference hands out free USB chargers and memory sticks with a supplier logo. What is the risk?

options.A: They are always safe because they are branded
options.B: They may run out of charge
options.C: They could contain malware or act as a keyboard to type commands
options.D: They might be the wrong colour

questions.explanation: Some devices look like storage or chargers but carry malicious code. Only use devices supplied or approved by your organisation.

questions.question: You need to move a large file to a colleague in another office. What is the most secure option?

options.A: Use the approved secure file-sharing service
options.B: Copy it to a personal USB stick
options.C: Post a printed copy
options.D: Upload it to a personal cloud account

questions.explanation: Approved services protect and track the data. Personal USB sticks are easily lost and are rarely encrypted.

questions.question: A contractor says their laptop has broken and asks to plug their own USB drive into your work PC to print a document urgently. What do you do?

options.A: Let them, they are in a hurry
options.B: Plug it in but do not open any files
options.C: Copy the file to your desktop first
options.D: Politely refuse and direct them to IT or an approved way to share the file

questions.explanation: An unknown drive can infect your PC the moment it connects. Being helpful should never mean bypassing device controls.

questions.question: Which statement about voice and video calls is true today?

options.A: Video calls cannot be faked
options.B: Only famous people can be impersonated
options.C: Voices and faces can be convincingly faked with AI
options.D: A familiar voice always proves who is calling

questions.explanation: AI tools can copy a voice from a short recording and fake a face on video. Familiar does not automatically mean genuine.

questions.question: Your director appears on a short video call asking you to move money urgently, but the picture is blurry and they refuse to turn the camera on properly. What is the warning sign?

options.A: The call happened in the afternoon
options.B: An urgent, unusual request with excuses not to be seen clearly
options.C: The director used your first name
options.D: The call used the company system

questions.explanation: Pressure plus an unusual request plus avoiding normal checks are classic signs of impersonation, whatever the voice sounds like.

questions.question: You receive a voice note that sounds exactly like your manager, asking for a customer list. What should you do?

options.A: Call your manager back on a known number to confirm
options.B: Send the list as the voice is familiar
options.C: Reply to the voice note asking if it is really them
options.D: Forward the voice note to the team

questions.explanation: Checking through a separate, trusted channel defeats voice cloning. Replying to the same channel just reaches the attacker.

questions.secure_behaviour: Keep Sensitive Data Out of Public AI Tools
questions.question: A colleague suggests pasting a confidential incident report into a free public AI chatbot to summarise it quickly before a meeting. What is the secure choice?

options.A: Paste it, it saves time
options.B: Paste only the first half
options.C: Use only approved AI tools and keep confidential data out of public ones
options.D: Paste it from a personal account instead

questions.explanation: Public AI tools may store or reuse what you type. Confidential data should only go into tools your organisation has approved.

questions.question: What is an insider threat?

options.A: A risk from someone inside the organisation who misuses their access
options.B: A virus that lives inside a computer
options.C: A storm damaging the building
options.D: A customer complaint

questions.explanation: Insider threats come from people with legitimate access, whether deliberate or accidental. Everyone plays a part in noticing them.

questions.question: A colleague who is leaving next week is downloading large amounts of customer data they do not normally use. What does this suggest?

options.A: They are being extra productive
options.B: Nothing, it is normal
options.C: Possible data theft that should be reported
options.D: They need a faster laptop

questions.explanation: Large, unusual downloads before someone leaves are a common warning sign. Reporting lets the right team look into it fairly.

questions.question: A colleague whose account is locked asks to use your login for the afternoon. What should you do?

options.A: Share it just this once
options.B: Write it down for them
options.C: Log in for them and leave the PC unlocked
options.D: Refuse and suggest they contact the IT service desk

questions.explanation: Shared logins mean any action is recorded against you, and they break the access controls that protect data.

questions.secure_behaviour: Report Concerns Through the Right Channel
questions.question: You notice a well-liked senior colleague copying confidential plans to a personal email address. Several people say it is probably fine. What should you do?

options.A: Say nothing to avoid awkwardness
options.B: Report it confidentially through the agreed reporting route
options.C: Confront them in front of the team
options.D: Post about it on a team chat

questions.explanation: Reporting through the proper route protects you, the organisation and the colleague, who may have an innocent explanation.

questions.question: Why should you report a suspected security incident quickly?

options.A: So you can be blamed
options.B: Early reporting limits the damage and helps others
options.C: It is only needed for big incidents
options.D: Reporting is optional

questions.explanation: The sooner the security team knows, the faster they can contain an attack. Small reports often reveal big problems.

questions.question: You clicked a link in a suspicious email but nothing seemed to happen. What is the right thing to do?

options.A: Report it anyway, as something may have happened in the background
options.B: Ignore it because nothing happened
options.C: Wait a week to see
options.D: Delete the email and forget it

questions.explanation: Many attacks run silently. A quick report lets experts check, and organisations want honest reports, not hidden mistakes.

questions.question: You receive a phishing email at work. What is the best way to report it?

options.A: Forward it to all colleagues as a warning
options.B: Reply to the sender saying you know it is fake
options.C: Use the official report-phishing button or process
options.D: Post a screenshot on social media

questions.explanation: The official route sends the email to the people who can block it for everyone. Forwarding or replying can spread the risk.

questions.question: You realise you sent a file with customer details to the wrong external address. Your team leader is busy and you are worried about getting into trouble. What should you do?

options.A: Hope the person deletes it
options.B: Wait until the end of the month
options.C: Ask the recipient to keep quiet
options.D: Report it immediately so the data breach process can start

questions.explanation: Data breaches often have legal time limits for reporting. Acting at once reduces harm, and honesty is valued over hiding mistakes.

questions.secure_behaviour: Check Who Can See Shared Files
questions.question: You share a folder using a link set to "Anyone with the link can view". What is the risk?

options.A: Nobody else can see it
options.B: Anyone who gets the link, inside or outside the organisation, can open it
options.C: Only your manager can see it
options.D: The files will be deleted

questions.explanation: Open links can be forwarded or found. Share with named people instead whenever the data is not public.

questions.question: An email says a colleague shared a document with you, but the sign-in page it opens has a slightly misspelled address. What should you do?

options.A: Do not enter your password; report it as phishing
options.B: Enter your password to see the document
options.C: Try a different password
options.D: Forward it to the colleague to open

questions.explanation: Fake sharing alerts are a common way to steal passwords. Always check the address before signing in.

questions.question: A partner company asks you to upload project files to their personal cloud storage account. What is the best response?

options.A: Upload everything to save time
options.B: Upload only some files
options.C: Use your organisation's approved file-sharing service instead
options.D: Email the files from a personal account

questions.explanation: Approved services keep control of the data and record who accessed it. Personal accounts sit outside that protection.

questions.secure_behaviour: Remove Access When It Is No Longer Needed
questions.question: A supplier's contract ended last month but they still have access to a shared folder with live operational data. Your colleague says it is too much work to change. What should you do?

options.A: Leave it in case they need it again
options.B: Change the folder name
options.C: Ask the supplier to promise not to look
options.D: Remove their access or ask the folder owner to do it now

questions.explanation: Old access is an easy route in for attackers. Removing it when it is no longer needed is a simple, powerful control.

questions.question: A supplier emails to say their bank details have changed for the next payment. What is the risk?

options.A: None, suppliers change banks often
options.B: It could be invoice fraud redirecting money to criminals
options.C: The payment will be late
options.D: The email may be too long

questions.explanation: Changing bank details by email is one of the most common frauds. Criminals often hack or copy a real supplier's email.

questions.question: An invoice arrives from "accounts@lochside-energy.co" instead of the usual ".co.uk" address. What does this suggest?

options.A: A lookalike address that may be fraudulent
options.B: A new office
options.C: A spelling mistake by IT
options.D: Nothing important

questions.explanation: Attackers register addresses that differ by a letter or ending. Small differences deserve a careful check.

questions.question: You are asked to update a supplier's bank details. What is the secure way to confirm the change?

options.A: Reply to the email asking if it is genuine
options.B: Check the email signature
options.C: Call the supplier on a number you already have on file
options.D: Call the number given in the email

questions.explanation: Use contact details you already trust, never those in the request itself, which the attacker controls.

questions.secure_behaviour: Follow the Payment Process Under Pressure
questions.question: Someone claiming to be the chief executive emails asking for an urgent confidential payment today and tells you not to involve finance. What should you do?

options.A: Pay it, the chief executive has authority
options.B: Pay a smaller amount first
options.C: Reply asking for more details then pay
options.D: Follow the normal approval process and verify the request independently

questions.explanation: Secrecy, urgency and authority together are the hallmarks of CEO fraud. Genuine leaders expect the process to be followed.
